newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy says it will not interfere in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: Italy says it will not interfere in Algeria.

text.p: Italy said on Friday that it had no intention of interfering in Algerian affairs after reports that it was preparing a peace initiative to halt the bloodshed.

Deputy foreign minister Piero Fassino said the international community, and in particular the European Union, had to "emerge from a condition of passivity and disinterest" and help Algeria end its civil strife "though without interference".
He denied that he had proposed "an 'international conference on Algeria', or any Italian or European mediation, as Algerian sources have claimed".

Fassino issued his statement after the newspaper L'Unita this week quoted him as saying in an interview that Italy planned to present a peace proposal on Algeria at a meeting of foreign ministers of Italy, Spain and France in February.
Algeria's military-backed government, locked in conflict with radical Islamists, has consistently rejected outside efforts to end five years of violence as interference.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini on Thursday said Italy wanted to see how it could contribute to resolving the crisis but had no intention of mediating.
"We are not going to interfere in what are their (Algerian) affairs. But we will always be present and will make our voice heard until the Algerian problem is resolved," Dini said.
Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf said on Friday that Italy's ambassador to Algeria had been summoned to the foreign ministry over Fassino's remarks in L'Unita.

Attaf said Algiers' envoy to Rome had been assured there was no Italian initiative on the North African country, that Italy barred itself from any interference in Algerian affairs, and that Rome's aim was to help isolate "terrorism" on the international level.

An estimated 60,000 people have been killed since Algeria plunged into civil strife after the authorities cancelled 1992 elections that the now outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had been poised to win.
A surge of violence has flared up during the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan which started on January 10. More than 170 people have died since then.

"...The very grave crisis Algeria is experiencing requires two things: a pact among all democratic Algerian political forces against terrorism and an agreement to conduct forthcoming parliamentary elections with the participation of all democratic forces," Fassino said in Friday's statement.

"...The international community, and first of all the European Union, must emerge from a condition of passivity and disinterest and help Algeria, though without interfering, to overcome the current crisis," he said.

Next month's meeting of the foreign ministers of Italy, France and Spain had been reported as scheduled for February 3. Diplomatic sources in Rome said it was now likely to take place in late February though no firm date had been set.
